questions.q: What must be configured before Athena will run any query at all?
options: A query result location — a separate S3 path where Athena writes query output
A Redshift cluster to temporarily stage the results
A Glue ETL job that runs before every query
A VPC endpoint dedicated solely to Athena traffic
questions.explain: Athena requires a configured S3 location for query results before it will execute anything.

questions.q: Why should the Athena query result location be a different S3 path from the raw data being queried?
options: Writing results into the raw zone risks the next crawler run picking up stray result files as if they were source data
Athena cannot technically write to the same bucket it reads from
AWS charges double for queries that read and write the same prefix
S3 only allows one object per prefix at a time
questions.explain: Keeping results in a separate location (northfield-athena-results) avoids contaminating the raw zone the crawler scans.

questions.q: What does `SELECT * FROM northfield_raw_db.orders_raw LIMIT 10;` actually prove when it runs successfully?
options: The entire chain — S3 files, the crawler's cataloged schema, and Athena's ability to query it — works end to end
That the stakeholder's business question has been fully answered
That the data has been successfully loaded into Redshift
That the raw CSV files have been converted to Parquet
questions.explain: This simple query is the proof point that the whole pipeline, from raw files to a queryable table, is functioning before tackling the real business question.

questions.q: How does Athena's pricing model actually work?
options: Billed by data scanned per query (roughly $5 per terabyte), with a 10 MB minimum per query, and nothing charged when no query runs
A fixed monthly subscription fee regardless of usage
Billed per hour that a dedicated cluster stays provisioned
Free for all queries under 1,000 rows returned, billed per row after that
questions.explain: Athena is a pay-per-query service billed on data scanned, which is why it costs close to nothing against a few megabytes of CSV.

questions.q: Why does the lesson flag that partitioning and file format will matter more as the raw zone grows?
options: Because Athena's cost is based on data scanned, so an unpartitioned, growing dataset means every query scans more data than it needs to
Because Athena has a hard limit of 31 files per table
Because Glue Crawlers charge more money for larger S3 prefixes
Because CSV files become unreadable past a certain total size
questions.explain: This sets up Lesson 8's partitioning lesson — as data grows, scanning everything to answer a narrow question gets slower and more expensive.
